nameStory: The 'bladderwort' name comes from the tiny bladder-like traps hidden underwater that this carnivorous plant uses to catch microscopic prey. The 'small swollen' part refers to its modest size compared to its bigger cousin, the swollen bladderwort, and the slightly inflated appearance of its floating stems.
description: Small swollen bladderwort is a fascinating floating carnivorous plant that lives entirely in the water. This medium-sized aquatic hunter can grow up to about a foot tall, drifting freely in ponds and lakes without any roots anchoring it to the bottom. What makes it truly special is that it's both a plant and a predator, using microscopic traps to catch tiny water creatures while also photosynthesizing like other plants.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Floats freely in water without any roots, forming loose, branching masses that feel soft and spongy when gently lifted from the water

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thread-like, highly divided underwater leaves that look like green feathers and feel delicate and slippery between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flowers on slender stalks that rise above the water surface, typically appearing in summer

idTips.label: Traps
idTips.description: Tiny bladder-like structures scattered along the underwater stems, barely visible but feeling like small bumps when you run your finger along the plant

habitat: Look for small swollen bladderwort in quiet freshwater areas like ponds, shallow lakes, and slow-moving ditches throughout New England. It prefers still or barely moving water where it can float freely without being swept away. You'll often find it mixed with other aquatic plants in areas with good sunlight penetration.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water temperatures warm, with fresh green shoots emerging from overwintering buds.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full development of the floating plant masses and yellow flowers appearing above water on thin stalks.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline as temperatures drop, forming winter buds that will survive the cold months.
seasonality.winter: Most of the plant dies back, surviving as small dormant buds (turions) that sink to the bottom and wait for spring.

funFact: This innocent-looking plant is actually a ruthless underwater predator that can suck in tiny water creatures faster than you can blink - its bladder traps create a vacuum that captures prey in less than a millisecond, making it one of the fastest hunters in the plant kingdom!
confusionNotes: Small swollen bladderwort is most easily confused with other floating bladderworts, especially common bladderwort, but it's smaller overall and lacks the distinctive inflated floats that some of its relatives have. Memory trick: if it's floating freely with feathery leaves but no obvious air-filled bladders keeping it up, you're likely looking at small swollen bladderwort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'carnivorous,' bladderworts don't actually digest their prey the way Venus flytraps do - instead, they absorb nutrients as the captured creatures decompose inside their tiny traps, supplementing what they get from photosynthesis in nutrient-poor waters.
compareHints: Small swollen bladderwort is smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort and lacks the large inflated floats of swollen bladderwort. Unlike purple bladderwort, which has purple flowers, this species always has yellow blooms. It's also more free-floating than some relatives that may have parts anchored to the bottom.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horned bladderwort stands out from its many bladderwort relatives by having the most prominent horn-like spur and by growing in terrestrial or semi-aquatic conditions rather than fully underwater.
Among New England's bladderworts, purple bladderwort is unique for its purple flowers – most others have yellow blooms.
Common bladderwort is the largest and most robust of New England's bladderworts, with the biggest flowers and most substantial underwater growth.
Swollen bladderwort is the largest of New England's aquatic bladderworts and the only one with truly prominent inflated stems that feel spongy to the touch.
Intermediate bladderwort differs from common bladderwort by having fewer, slightly smaller flowers and more delicate overall appearance.
Humped bladderwort is much smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort, forming thin surface mats rather than robust underwater colonies.
Northeastern bladderwort is distinguished from other New England bladderworts by its lavender-purple flowers and preference for very shallow water or bog margins.

Hidden-fruit Bladderwort is unique among New England's bladderworts for keeping its flowers at or below the water surface, while most relatives like Common and Purple Bladderwort hold their blooms well above water on conspicuous stalks.
Lesser bladderwort is distinguished from common bladderwort by its much smaller size and more delicate appearance overall.
Among New England's bladderworts, zigzag bladderwort is unique for its terrestrial zigzag growth habit - most other bladderworts either float in water or grow upright from water.
Distinguished from common bladderwort by much finer, more delicate underwater stems and smaller overall size.
